title: Eccles Cakes
subtitle: flaky puff pastry rounds filled with spiced currants
excerpt: Eccles cakes are small, round pastries filled with a buttery spiced currant mixture and encased in puff pastry. They have a sugary, caramelised crust and a rich, jammy interior. They go very well with Lancashire cheese.
sourceNotes: Named after the town of Eccles in Greater Manchester. The recipe dates to at least the 18th century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked. Bake from frozen at 200C adding 5 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling can be made 3 days ahead and kept in the fridge.

content.text: The key technique is enclosing the filling completely -- any gaps will leak during baking. Gather the pastry edges to the centre and press firmly to seal, then flip the parcel over so the seam is underneath before pressing flat. Score the top with three cuts so steam can escape.
Mix together the softened butter, brown sugar, currants, allspice, and nutmeg to make the filling. Set aside.
On a lightly floured surface, roll the puff pastry to about 3mm thick. Cut out 12 rounds with a 10cm cutter.
Place a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of each round. Gather the pastry edges up over the filling, pressing and pinching to seal completely. Flip over so the seam is underneath.
Gently flatten each parcel with the palm of your hand to about 1cm thick. Place on lined baking sheets. Chill for 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 200C. Brush each cake with milk and scatter with caster sugar. Score three cuts across the top. Bake for 18 to 20 minutes until deep golden. Cool slightly before eating.

items.cause: Pastry was not sealed tightly enough.
items.fix: Press the edges firmly together and check there are no gaps before flipping. The seam should be firmly underneath.

items.symptom: Pastry is pale and not flaky
items.cause: Pastry was too warm when going into the oven.
items.fix: Chill the assembled cakes for 15 minutes before baking. Cold pastry creates steam, which creates layers.

content.text: Eccles cakes come from the town of Eccles in Greater Manchester and have been made there since at least 1793. They are one of the most distinctive regional bakes in England -- sticky, flaky, and intensely fruity. The traditional pairing with a strong Lancashire cheese is one of those combinations that sounds odd and tastes extraordinary.
